title: That the profit of one man is the damage of another
paragraphs: Demades the Athenian condemned one of his fellow citizens whose trade it was to sell the necessaries for funeral ceremonies, on the pretext that he was demanding unreasonable profit, and that this profit could only come from the death of a great many people. A judgment that seems ill-founded, since no profit whatever can be made except at someone else's expense; by the same rule he ought to condemn all gain of any kind. The merchant only thrives by the debauchery of youth, the husbandman by the dearness of grain, the architect by the ruin of buildings, lawyers and officers of justice by the lawsuits and quarrels of men; even the dignity and office of divines is derived from our death and our vices. "A physician takes no pleasure in the health even of his friends," says the ancient Greek comic writer; nor a soldier in the peace of his country; and so on with the rest. And, what is worse, let everyone but dive into his own bosom and he will find his private wishes spring and his secret hopes grow up at someone else's expense. Reflecting on this, it comes into my head that nature does not in this depart from her general policy; for physicians hold that the birth, nourishment, and increase of every thing is the dissolution and corruption of another:
"Nam quodcumque suis mutatum finibus exit, Continuo hoc mors est illius, quod fuit ante."
["For whatever passes changed from its own bounds, this is at once the death of that which it was before." — Lucretius, ii. 752.]
